name: Tai Chi and Qigong programs (Tai Chi for Health Institute; Spring Forest Qigong)
founders: Paul Lam, MD (Sydney family physician, UNSW graduate 1974; Tai Chi for Arthritis 1997; Tai Chi for Health Institute 2010)
founded_year_range: 1995-2010 for the branded programs: SFQ 'since 1995', Tai Chi for Arthritis 1997, TCHI 2010 (per official sites). The underlying traditions are centuries old.
cost_summary: TCHI is a non-profit instructor-certification network. Its community classes are often free or low-cost through Older Americans Act/AAA-funded senior programs (typical, not verified per site). It earns from paid 1-2-day instructor workshops and DVDs (prices not shown on its home page). Spring Forest Qigong is commercial: online courses, monthly subscriptions and 'karmic cleansing' (prices not shown), and a 5-day Intensive Healing Retreat at USD 3,295-3,800 (site, 2026). Generic tai chi/qigong is available free on YouTube or as paid local classes.
mechanisms: autonomic/nervous system dysregulation (sympathetic overdrive, "stuck in fight-or-flight")
mechanism_summary: Traditionally, illness reflects blocked or imbalanced qi, and slow movement, breath and intention restore its flow. Spring Forest Qigong adds energy-healing claims. Researchers frame it as multicomponent meditative movement: gentle aerobic, balance and strength exercise with graded exposure to movement; parasympathetic/vagal up-regulation through slow breathing; HPA-axis and inflammatory down-regulation; mindfulness-like body awareness and interoception; and self-efficacy and social support. Fibromyalgia trialists hypothesise effects on central sensitization, but this was not tested mechanistically. No disease-specific mechanisms are proposed.
techniques: Sun-style 12-movement Tai Chi for Arthritis form
SFQ Level 1 Active Exercises (6 movements) + guided audio meditation, 30-60 min daily
SFQ Qi-ssage self-massage, healing circles, energy healing
group classes 1-2x/week for 8-24 weeks plus home practice
mainstream_notes: Several guidelines recommend tai chi: the ACP 2017 guideline lists it as a nonpharmacologic option for chronic low back pain, the ACR/AF 2019 guideline strongly recommends it for knee and hip OA, and EULAR 2016 rates meditative movement for fibromyalgia as weak-for. AHRQ reviews (Skelly 2018/2020) include it. CDC and the Arthritis Foundation recommend Tai Chi for Arthritis (and Fall Prevention), and it appears on ACL/NCOA evidence-based program lists. It is offered in VA Whole Health and academic integrative centres (general knowledge, not re-verified). The Yang 2024 virtual LBP RCT had Mayo co-authors but was industry-funded by the lead author's company, so it is not evidence of Mayo adoption. Spring Forest Qigong's mainstream adoption is limited: University of Minnesota feasibility studies only.
insurance_notes: Tai chi has no CPT code of its own. Access comes indirectly through Medicare Advantage fitness benefits (e.g., SilverSneakers class menus), Older Americans Act Title III-D funding for evidence-based programs, the VA, and employer wellness programs (general knowledge; not re-fetched). Qigong energy healing is not reimbursed.

key_trials.citation: Wang C et al. A randomized trial of tai chi for fibromyalgia. N Engl J Med 2010;363:743-754. PMID 20818876
key_trials.design: Single-blind RCT, classic Yang-style tai chi vs wellness education + stretching, 12 wk, 2x60 min/wk
key_trials.finding: FIQ fell 18.4 points more than control (p<0.001), and the gap held at 24 weeks (-18.3). SF-36 physical and mental scores improved. No adverse events.

key_trials.citation: Wang C et al. Effect of tai chi versus aerobic exercise for fibromyalgia: comparative effectiveness RCT. BMJ 2018;360:k851. PMID 29563100
key_trials.design: Single-blind comparative-effectiveness RCT, 4 Yang-style tai chi dose arms (12 or 24 wk, 1x or 2x/wk) vs aerobic exercise 24 wk; 52-wk follow-up
key_trials.finding: Combined tai chi beat aerobic exercise on FIQR at 24 wk: difference 5.5 (95% CI 0.6-10.4), and 16.2 at equal dose. 24 wk of tai chi beat 12 wk; 2x/wk was not better than 1x/wk. Tai chi attendance was higher.

key_trials.citation: Jones KD et al. A randomized controlled trial of 8-form Tai chi improves symptoms and functional mobility in fibromyalgia patients. Clin Rheumatol 2012;31:1205-14. PMID 22581278
key_trials.design: RCT, FM-modified 8-form Yang-style tai chi vs education, 2x90 min/wk for 12 wk
key_trials.finding: FIQ improved 16.5 vs 3.1 (p=0.0002), with gains in pain, sleep, self-efficacy and mobility. No adverse events.

key_trials.citation: Hall AM, Maher CG, Lam P, Ferreira M, Latimer J. Tai chi exercise for treatment of pain and disability in people with persistent low back pain: RCT. Arthritis Care Res 2011;63:1576-83. PMID 22034119
key_trials.design: Pragmatic RCT, tai chi (Paul Lam co-author) vs waitlist, 18 x 40 min over 10 wk
key_trials.finding: Bothersomeness fell 1.7/10, pain 1.3/10 and RMDQ 2.6/24 vs waitlist.

key_trials.citation: Callahan LF et al. Evaluation of Tai Chi Program Effectiveness for People with Arthritis in the Community: RCT. J Aging Phys Act 2016;24:101-10. PMID 26099162
key_trials.design: Community RCT of the Arthritis Foundation Tai Chi Program (AF-licensed Tai Chi for Arthritis) vs waitlist, 8 wk; 1-yr self-report follow-up
key_trials.finding: Balance by reach (ES 0.30) and helplessness, sleep and role satisfaction (ES 0.24-0.54) improved. Pain, fatigue and stiffness (ES 0.15-0.23) only approached significance. No change in mobility, strength or single-leg balance. Gains were maintained at 1 yr (uncontrolled).

key_trials.citation: Lynch M, Sawynok J, Hiew C, Marcon D. A randomized controlled trial of qigong for fibromyalgia. Arthritis Res Ther 2012;14:R178. PMID 22863206
key_trials.design: RCT, immediate vs delayed Chaoyi Fanhuan qigong vs waitlist/usual care, 8 wk + 45-60 min/day home practice, 6-mo follow-up
key_trials.finding: Pain, impact, sleep and physical and mental function improved, sustained to 6 mo. A post hoc per-protocol analysis found more benefit with fuller practice.

key_trials.citation: Chan JS et al. Effects of qigong exercise on fatigue, anxiety, and depressive symptoms of patients with CFS-like illness: RCT. eCAM 2013:485341. PMID 23983785
key_trials.design: RCT, qigong (Baduanjin) 10 sessions over 5 wk + 12 wk home practice vs waitlist
key_trials.finding: Total and physical fatigue and depression fell. Mental fatigue was marginal (p=0.05). Anxiety did not change.

key_trials.citation: Ho RT et al. RCT of qigong exercise on fatigue symptoms, functioning, and telomerase activity in persons with chronic fatigue or CFS. Ann Behav Med 2012;44:160-70. PMID 22736201
key_trials.finding: Fatigue and mental functioning improved, and telomerase activity rose. Physical functioning was not reported as improved.

key_trials.citation: Markwart M et al. Qigong and Tai Chi for ME/CFS: A Systematic Review of RCTs. Glob Adv Integr Med Health 2024;13:27536130241275607. PMID 39524182
key_trials.finding: 5 qigong RCTs (2012-2023) and no tai chi RCTs found. Verdict: promising yet understudied; calls for standardized ME/CFS eligibility criteria.

key_trials.citation: Wang C et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Tai Chi Versus Physical Therapy for Knee Osteoarthritis. Ann Intern Med 2016;165:77-86. PMID 27183035
key_trials.design: RCT, tai chi vs PT, 12 wk
key_trials.finding: WOMAC improvement was equivalent. Tai chi improved depression more.

key_trials.citation: Yang Y et al. A Tai chi and qigong mind-body program for low back pain: a virtually delivered RCT. N Am Spine Soc J 2024;20:100557. PMID 39469294
key_trials.design: RCT, 12-wk live-online Chen-style tai chi + Hunyuan qigong + meditation (2x60 min/wk) vs waitlist; led by Center for Taiji and Qigong Studies (NY), funded by the lead author's company Qi Balance LLC; Mayo/Weill Cornell co-authors
key_trials.finding: ODI improved by 4.7 at 8 wk, 6.4 at 12 wk and 8.1 at 16 wk vs control (p<.01). About 30% attrition.

key_trials.citation: Dietzel J et al. Acupressure and Qigong in post-infectious fatigue with impaired physical function: a randomized clinical trial. Front Med (Lausanne) 2026;13:1872035. PMID 42638691
key_trials.design: Open-label RCT (ACUQiG, Charite Berlin), 8 wk daily self-acupressure + twice-weekly online qigong vs self-care leaflet, post-COVID fatigue
key_trials.finding: Null on primary outcome: SF-36 physical function difference 4.2 (95% CI -0.9 to 9.4, p=0.11). Chalder fatigue slightly better (p=0.04). Some symptom aggravation occurred.

key_trials.citation: Coleman JF. Spring Forest Qigong and chronic pain: making a difference. J Holist Nurs 2011;29:118-28. PMID 21062951
key_trials.design: Uncontrolled mixed-methods pilot, SFQ Level 1, 30 min/day x 8 wk (122 oriented, 86 analysed)
key_trials.finding: Reported significant symptom improvement. No control group, and the abstract gives no effect sizes.

controversy: Qi and meridian theory has no demonstrated physical basis. Spring Forest Qigong's energy-healing, distant-healing and 'karmic cleansing' offerings, and its testimonials of cancer and Parkinson's recovery, are unsupported. The Chinese qigong-fever era included fraudulent masters. The trials cannot blind participants, mostly use waitlist or education controls, are often small and high-risk-of-bias, and are highly heterogeneous. Several trials were run or funded by practitioners (Yang 2024 by the lead author's company; Lam co-authored Hall 2011). The ME/CFS qigong trials come mostly from one Hong Kong group using 'CFS-like illness' samples without PEM criteria. The first large long-COVID RCT (Dietzel 2026) was null on its primary outcome and reported some symptom aggravation. TCHI's 'CDC-supported' marketing applies to arthritis and falls only, not to its other condition-labelled programs. The best branded-program trial (Callahan 2016) found only modest effects, with pain not significantly improved.

popularity.reach_estimate: Tens of millions cumulatively for tai chi/qigong in the West (NHIS: roughly 1-2% of US adults practise; unverified figure). Lam programs claim >10 million (self-reported, unaudited). Spring Forest Qigong probably 10^4-10^5 (no published numbers).
popularity.method_notes: Umbrella entry with a long pre-1970 baseline (mass practice in China; Western spread from the 1970s). The trajectory has these steps: Spring Forest Qigong 'since 1995'; Tai Chi for Arthritis launched 1997; DVDs in the 2000s; NCCAM-funded trials and CDC/AF endorsement in the late 2000s; NEJM fibromyalgia trial and TCHI founding in 2010; BMJ trial media spike in 2018; COVID-era virtual classes and qigong long-COVID trials in 2020-26. After that it plateaus. Reach combines Lam's self-reported >10M and approximate NHIS prevalence. NHIS and Google Trends values come from general knowledge and were not re-fetched, because the web-search budget was exhausted (during both research and fact-check). Reddit and social-media metrics were not gathered.
